edges.description: Overexpression of the wild-type protein alone produces abnormal motor function and reduced conduction velocity, which is the observation the dosage hypothesis rests on.
edges.limitations: Fidelity is LOW as a model of human CMT1G because no patient has been reported with PMP2 overexpression or duplication - every human allele is a missense or in-frame deletion. The model demonstrates that excess P2 is sufficient to cause neuropathy in mouse; it does not show that this is the mechanism in patients.

edges.description: Loss of PMP2 does not reproduce the human demyelinating phenotype. Whatever the human alleles do, abolishing the protein is not it.
edges.limitations: A mouse null is not the human genotype: every reported human allele is a heterozygous missense or in-frame deletion, so the model tests a genetic situation no patient has. Mouse peripheral myelin may also tolerate loss of P2 better than human myelin does - the two species' myelin protein stoichiometries differ - so a null being near-normal in mouse does not establish that a human null would be. The finding constrains the mechanism; it does not settle it.

edges.description: Ablating PMP2+ Schwann cells causes loss of large-caliber motor axons with behavioural, electrophysiological and ultrastructural deficits, and restoring the cells reverses much of it.
edges.limitations: This is cell ablation, not a PMP2 variant: the Schwann cells are killed rather than made to express a mutant protein, so it models the consequence of losing the cell type, not the consequence of the human allele. It also speaks to motor axon survival rather than to the demyelination that defines CMT1G, and the paper's framing is ALS rather than CMT.

nodes.description:
A parallel mechanistic claim, and the most surprising finding in this literature. In the transgenic experiment, mice overexpressing wild-type P2 developed abnormal motor function, reduced motor nerve conduction velocity and shortened internodes just as the p.I43N animals did. That is the same pattern PMP22 shows, where duplication rather than a coding change causes CMT1A, and it suggests myelin is sensitive to P2 dose as such.
Graded HYPOTHETICAL for human CMT1G because no patient has been reported with a PMP2 duplication or with overexpression - the finding is a property of a transgenic overexpression system, and the authors themselves call for further mechanistic work. It is curated because it is the strongest available constraint on how the human missense alleles act.
